title: Milestone: Atoms to Molecules
objective: After this level you can connect atoms, elements and bonds into one picture of matter.
summary: Atoms hold on three ways: ionic bonds trade electrons, covalent bonds share them, metallic bonds pool them. A substance's properties reveal which bonds hold it together.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Let's build matter from the atom up.
cards.body: Chapter 1 said everything is made of particles. This chapter showed how atoms hold on to each other. Put the two together and you can read a material like a detective.

items.label: Ionic (table salt)
points: Electrons handed over; ions in a grid
Hard and brittle, melts only when very hot
Conducts only when melted or dissolved

items.label: Covalent (water, oxygen)
points: Electrons shared in pairs, making molecules
Often a gas, a liquid or a low-melting solid

items.label: Metallic (any metal)
points: Electrons pooled in a free-moving sea
Conducts as a solid; bends instead of shattering

cards.headline: Read the clues
cards.body: Now try it. A shiny solid that bends under a hammer and carries a current: metallic bonds. A hard, brittle crystal that melts only when very hot: ionic. A gas at room temperature, like the nitrogen in the air: small molecules, held together by covalent bonds. Chapter 1's particles plus this chapter's bonds explain why a spoon bends, salt shatters, snowflakes are six-fold and plastic stretches into chains.

cards.headline: Milestone: atoms to molecules
learned: Ionic bonds trade electrons, covalent share, metallic pool
Shape and polarity explain water's quirks
Crystals and polymers are atoms bonded on a grand scale

questions.prompt: Atoms-to-molecules review: which bond forms when one atom hands an electron to another, as in table salt?

options.label: A covalent bond
options.rationale: Covalent bonds share electrons rather than hand them over.

options.label: A metallic bond
options.rationale: Metals pool electrons in a shared sea.

options.label: An ionic bond
A hydrogen bond
options.rationale: That's a weaker pull between whole molecules.

questions.explanation: Sodium hands an electron to chlorine, and the resulting opposite ions attract: an ionic bond.

questions.prompt: Chapter 1 said all matter is made of tiny particles. How does this chapter describe the particles of water?

options.label: Single atoms of an element called water
options.rationale: Water is made of two elements bonded together.

options.label: Ions stacked in a grid, like table salt
options.rationale: Water comes in molecules, not an ion grid.

options.label: Long chains of repeating units
options.rationale: That describes polymers.

options.label: Molecules of two hydrogens bonded to one oxygen

questions.explanation: Water's particles are molecules, each with two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

questions.prompt: Which gas in the air is held together by a triple bond?

options.label: Oxygen
options.rationale: Oxygen gas has a double bond.

options.label: Nitrogen
Hydrogen
options.rationale: Hydrogen gas has a single bond.

options.label: None; gases have only single bonds
options.rationale: Oxygen's double and nitrogen's triple bonds say otherwise.

questions.explanation: Nitrogen gas, about 78 percent of the air, has a very strong triple bond, which keeps it unreactive.

questions.prompt: An unknown solid is shiny, bends when hammered and conducts electricity as a solid. What holds it together?

options.label: Ionic bonds
options.rationale: Ionic solids shatter and conduct only when melted or dissolved.

options.label: Hydrogen bonds
options.rationale: Those are weak pulls between molecules.

options.label: Metallic bonds
Covalent bonds in small molecules
options.rationale: Those substances are usually gases, liquids or low-melting solids.

questions.explanation: Conducting as a solid and bending instead of shattering are the signs of a metal's electron sea.

questions.prompt: Why don't methane's four hydrogen atoms lie flat around the carbon?

options.label: Hydrogen atoms are too heavy to lie flat
options.rationale: Weight has nothing to do with it.

options.label: Their electron pairs repel and spread out
The carbon pulls them into a straight line
options.rationale: Methane is a tetrahedron, not a line.

options.label: Methane is an ionic crystal with a cubic grid
options.rationale: Methane is a covalent molecule.

questions.explanation: Electron pairs around a central atom repel and spread as far apart as possible, giving methane its tetrahedral shape.

questions.prompt: Ice floats, and every snowflake has six-fold symmetry. What do both come from?

options.label: Salt dissolved in rain and seawater
options.rationale: Pure ice floats and forms snowflakes too.

options.label: Air trapped between the ice crystals
options.rationale: The explanation is in the molecules' arrangement.

options.label: The pattern water molecules lock into as they freeze
Water turning into ions when it freezes
options.rationale: Ice is still water molecules.

questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonds lock freezing water into an open, hexagonal lattice: less dense than the liquid, and six-fold in every snowflake.

questions.prompt: Level 6 said a solution is the same all the way through. In salt water, what is spread evenly among the water molecules?

options.label: Tiny whole cubes of salt crystal
options.rationale: Dissolving takes the crystal apart.

options.label: Sodium and chloride ions pulled apart by water
Salt molecules, each made of two atoms
options.rationale: Salt has no molecules.

options.label: Bubbles of chlorine gas
options.rationale: No gas forms when salt dissolves.

questions.explanation: Polar water molecules pull salt's grid apart, and the sodium and chloride ions spread evenly through the water.
